claims.text: Reported HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure containing multiple phases and well-defined interfaces.
Grain-size distributions, phase fractions, and interface metrics can be quantitatively extracted from high-resolution imaging of HfNbTiVAl10.
The extracted descriptors will be integrated into a machine-learning model coupled with continuum simulation.
The integrated approach will reduce computation time by at least 50% relative to established simulations.
The integrated approach will reduce prediction error for Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture parameters by at least 20% relative to conventional simulations.
The spatial arrangement and phase distribution of nanoscale and microscale features mediate local stress concentrations.
The hierarchical heterostructure mediates deformation pathways.
Microstructural features govern local elastic and plastic deformation.
Encoding critical microstructural features will let the model correlate heterogeneity more directly with macroscopic mechanical responses.
The data-driven framework can bypass lengthy iterative physical simulations.
The conventional baseline methods do not explicitly incorporate detailed heterostructural descriptors.
Conventional physical simulations assume idealized homogeneity.
The framework is intended for uniaxial tensile and standardized fracture tests at room temperature and possibly moderately elevated temperatures under controlled strain rates.
Processing variability could prevent reproducible extraction of heterostructural descriptors and cause the hypothesis to fail.
A training set that does not span the full range of microstructural variability could cause prediction failure.
Extreme loading or high temperatures may induce additional microstructural evolution outside the model's training domain.
The achieved accuracy and time gains will depend on imaging resolution, descriptor-extraction quality, and training-data quality.
Overfitting or insufficient sensitivity to minor heterogeneity variations may limit generalizability.
Young's modulus can be measured for the validation study using ultrasonic or acoustic-emission testing.
Failure to achieve either a 20% reduction in prediction error or a 50% reduction in computation time in independent tests will falsify the hypothesis.
